title: Pull the Plug
briefing: Same traffic as before: up to 5,000 requests per second, 10ms of CPU each.
About a minute in, one of your app servers will crash. Machines die all the time in production, and your design has to keep serving through it.

Load balancers find dead instances with health checks: every few seconds they probe each instance, and take it out of rotation after 2 failed checks in a row. Until then, they keep sending it traffic.
debrief: Surviving a crash takes two things.
Spare capacity, known as N+1: if you need 4 servers to carry the load, run 5. When one dies, the rest still keep up. With only 4, the 3 survivors are overloaded for the rest of the run.

Fast failover: even with a 5-second health-check interval, the load balancer needs 2 failed checks, up to 10 seconds, to notice. Meanwhile 1 in 5 requests goes to a dead machine. That's 1/5 × 9s ≈ 1.8 seconds' worth of traffic lost out of 180, about 1% of requests: 99% availability, below the 99.9% needed to pass.

Retries close the gap. A crashed server refuses connections immediately, so the load balancer can retry the request on another instance about a millisecond later, and the user never notices. Retrying is safe here because the request never reached the application. Retrying requests that might already have been processed is a harder problem, which comes up in later levels.
Health checks keep the dead server out of rotation; retries cover the gap until they do. You need both.

solutions.name: N+1 xlarge servers with retries
solutions.explanation: Five xlarge servers where four would do. When one crashes, the remaining 64 vCPUs run at 78%. Retries hide the crash from users until health checks remove the dead server.

solutions.name: Ten large servers with retries
solutions.explanation: Smaller machines make each failure smaller: losing one of ten costs 10% of capacity, not 20%. Retries do the rest, so even the default 30-second health check is fine.

antiSolutions.name: N+1 with fast health checks, no retries
antiSolutions.explanation: The load balancer needs about 9 seconds to notice the crash. Until then a fifth of all requests hit a dead server.

antiSolutions.name: N+1 with default health checks, no retries
antiSolutions.explanation: With 30-second checks, the dead server keeps getting a fifth of the traffic for almost a minute.

antiSolutions.name: Exactly enough servers, with retries
antiSolutions.explanation: Four xlarge servers carry 5,000 req/s comfortably until one dies. Then 3 servers face 5,000 req/s with capacity for 4,800.
